description: SPHEREx is expected to drive significant advances in astronomy and other fields of science. An important first step toward realizing this potential is to process and refine its data, making it more accessible and useful. Through this project, we aim to encourage broader participation in citizen science and enable more people to contribute to scientific research and future discoveries.
summary:
Every six months, NASA's SPHEREx maps the whole sky in 102 infrared colors, but its archive is daunting for newcomers. Built on real SPHEREx data, ApogeeX lets anyone explore that sky and study asteroids' spectra, size, albedo and 3D orbits in a browser.
A Stellarium-based planetarium sends any box drawn on the sky to an observation workbench, where SPHEREx images blink in date order on one north-up grid. For the five challenge targets, A−B differences highlight motion and variability, a cold-object filter cancels ordinary stars, leaving cold objects like the brown dwarf WISE 0855−0714. A 3D model moves its camera to Earth's position at each exposure, so the scene matches the image.The asteroid lab places asteroids on JPL Horizons orbits and replays SPHEREx frames from the spacecraft's viewpoint. A Python pipeline extracts 0.75–5 µm spectra, calibrates them with solar-analog stars and separates reflected sunlight from thermal glow (NEATM), yielding spectral type, diameter and albedo with uncertainties.Tutorials guide beginners and researchers. Every value is labeled as measured, catalogue or model, and failed downloads are never replaced with sample data, so users learn to check the evidence before calling anything a discovery.
details:
ApogeeX: watch the infrared sky change, then check what really changed

SPHEREx maps the entire sky in 102 infrared colors every six months. That makes it a time machine for the nearby universe: stars that move, stars that pulse, and asteroids that cross a field within hours. ApogeeX lets anyone see those changes in real SPHEREx images and then test them with the same checks a researcher would use.

TRY IT!

1. Open the English workbench for Barnard's Star, or choose SPHEREx Analysis in the site menu and pick Barnard's Star. Press play: 17 real SPHEREx visits from August 2025 to September 2026 blink on one north-up grid. The star moves about 10.4″ per year, roughly 1.7 SPHEREx pixels, while background stars stay put.

2. Choose WISE 0855−0714, the coldest known brown dwarf (about 250–285 K). With all wavelengths combined it is nearly lost in starlight. Switch to D6 (4.4–5.0 µm), then turn on the cold-object filter: ordinary stars fade away and the cold object's 4.5 µm light is what remains to inspect.

3. Press "◎ SPHEREx line of sight". The 3D camera flies to Earth's position on the observation date and looks down the telescope's field, the 3D star lands on the image's predicted marker.

4. Press "Analyse" to open Research mode. The position tab plots measured-minus-predicted offsets with 1σ error bars, the data-source tab lists every visit's IRSA files and exports them as CSV.

5. Open Asteroid Analysis , pick 433 Eros and choose "SPHEREx view" : the camera jumps to the spacecraft's real position at that exposure, and the fixed-sky replay shows the asteroid crossing real frames. This screen is in Korean.

WHAT ApogeeX DOES

- Planetarium. interface adds controls for location, time speed, projection and coordinate grids, an all-sky Mollweide view and share links. Clicking a star shows information, our "SPHEREx analysis" box tool sends the selected patch's ICRS center and size to the workbench.

- SPHEREx Analysis ("Armchair Astronomer"). Blink player (up to 8 fps, step, A/B swap), A−B difference images, a D1–D6 spectral ruler, the cold-object filter, a synchronized 3D space-time model, Explore mode mission cards for each target, and Research mode labs for variability, spectra, positions and provenance. A live sky map streams the SPHEREx all-sky cube with a 102-channel wavelength slider, and Gaia DR3 stars can be overlaid at each observation date.

- Asteroid Analysis. A 3D Solar System with 24 asteroids and 8 planets on JPL Horizons orbits, 98 real SPHEREx imaging scenes for 23 asteroids, ePSF model overlays, predicted per-exposure positions, and a Python pipeline for spectra, taxonomy, diameter, H and albedo. Prepared results open in the browser.

- Search and tutorials. One search bar for 19,975 named objects in Korean or English and for decimal or sexagesimal coordinates. Six tutorial modules, each with a beginner and a researcher track, guide characters, quizzes and practice steps on the real screens.

HOW IT WORKS

Each prepared target's position comes from Gaia DR3 (or the literature for WISE 0855, which is too faint for Gaia) and is moved to every observation date. A preparation script finds SPHEREx DR1/QR3 Level-2 exposures through IRSA TAP, downloads small cutouts, masks bad-pixel flags, removes the background and reprojects everything onto one fixed north-up 6.15″/pixel grid, so any movement in the blink is real sky movement. For new coordinates, a Python service builds the same kind of frames on demand for fields 0.025–0.5° wide. It runs locally or on a separately hosted server, so the public static site offers the five prepared targets. Asteroids are found with IRSA MOST and JPL Horizons using SPHEREx itself as the observer, then measured with forced PSF photometry from 0.75 to 5 µm.

WHAT WE CHECKED ON REAL DATA

- Cold-object filter. In five wide WISE 0855 visits, bright field stars had a median D6/D5 ratio of 0.71–0.80, matching the Rayleigh–Jeans value of 0.77. After filtering, their median residual was −0.08 to +0.04, close to zero. Visits with few D6 exposures can keep cosmic-ray hits, and the screen says so. The filter is a color selection, not an identification.

- 3D geometry. For every visit of every target, the 3D camera's projection of the star matches the predicted image pixel to within 0.5 px (in practice under 0.01 px, because a perspective camera and the gnomonic image projection are the same mathematics).

- Asteroid positions. For 433 Eros (218 exposures), Horizons positions computed from SPHEREx agree with IRSA MOST to 0.2″ and with the measured image peak to about 0.1 px. PSF fluxes agree with aperture sums to 1–3%.

- Spectral calibration. A correction built from 14 solar-analog stars (1,657 clean points) passes a split-sample test (χ²/N = 0.91).

- Diameters. Across 23 asteroids, the median 1σ uncertainty is 16%, and the rms difference from catalogue diameters is 0.072 dex (about 18%). Six hold-out asteroids that were never used for tuning all fall within 2σ of their catalogue values.

- An honest exception. For Eros, our thermal diameter is 24.1 km against NEAR's volume-equivalent 16.8 km. SPHEREx saw the elongated body nearly pole-on, and the effective diameter of NEAR's shape model at that geometry is 22.1 km, within 0.4σ of our value. ApogeeX shows the comparison instead of hiding it.

- Software. 713 automated checks pass (11 skipped because they need live archives or special setups, 0 failed).

THE FIVE CHALLENGE TARGETS

- Barnard's Star: 17 visits, the fastest-moving star on the sky, about 1.7 pixels per year.

- Epsilon Indi B: 19 visits, a brown-dwarf pair 0.7″ apart, seen as one point moving about 4.7″ per year; Gaia's RUWE warning is shown.

- WISE 0855−0714: 9 visits, positions are measured only in D5–D6, because nearby stars pull the centroid by 1.2–1.8 px at shorter wavelengths.

- RW Aurigae: 7 visits, a nearly fixed control, studied through its brightness; Gaia's RUWE warning is shown.

- R Draconis: 47 visits, a Mira variable, explored in the light-curve lab with trial-period folding and a published reference period.

WHAT THE CHALLENGE ASKS, AND WHERE IT IS IN ApogeeX

1. Enter coordinates: yes. Names, decimal degrees or sexagesimal in the search bar, or a box drawn in the planetarium. On the live site, the five prepared targets open immediately, images for new coordinates are built when the Python service is running.

2. Play images like a short video: yes. Blink playback in date order, up to 8 fps, with stepping and A/B swap.

3. Easy to update: yes. The preparation script rebuilds the prepared targets, with the Python service running, new fields are fetched from IRSA on demand and the asteroid pipeline accepts new targets and date ranges.

4. 102 bands and spectra: yes. A 102-channel all-sky slider, a D1–D6 ruler, a spectrum lab for the prepared targets, and 0.75–5 µm asteroid spectra.

5. Add or subtract dates: yes. Exposures are averaged within each visit, and A−B differences compare dates, a difference is withheld when the two dates share no wavelength coverage.

6. Choose the field of view: yes. 0.1° and 0.3° frames for the prepared targets on the live site, 0.025–0.5° for new fields (set by the planetarium box) when the Python service is running.

7. Other telescopes and catalogues: partly. Gaia DR3 star overlay, a Gaia-versus-SPHEREx all-sky comparison, the DSS photo layer in the planetarium, and SIMBAD names.

8. Coordinates in the URL: yes. ra, dec and fov open a field, target, mode, tab and visit restore the exact view, "Copy link" shares it.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Prepared targets open in any modern browser with no account or installation, and every number traces back to an IRSA file. Beginners learn to read wavelengths, light curves and error bars through short guided tutorials, researchers get provenance tables, quality masks and CSV exports. The interface is in Korean, with a full English mode in the analysis workbench, so Korean-speaking students and amateur astronomers can work with NASA mission data in their own language. Above all, we want users to leave with a scientist's habit: before calling something a discovery, check its wavelength, its quality flags and where it came from.

TOOLS

- Languages: TypeScript, JavaScript and Python 3.11, with a Node.js 22 gateway and SQLite.

- Open-source software we used: the Stellarium Web Engine (AGPL-3.0) for the planetarium, three.js (MIT), React, react-three-fiber, zustand and Vite for the browser interface, Astropy, astroquery, PyVO, reproject, NumPy, SciPy, pandas, scikit-learn, sbpy, synphot and Matplotlib for data processing, Vitest, Playwright and pytest for testing. Each component keeps its own open-source license, and the license notices of the components bundled into the website are published with it.

- Open map data: capital-city coordinates from GeoNames (CC BY 4.0) and city labels from Natural Earth (public domain).

- Science data: NASA/IPAC IRSA SPHEREx DR1/QR3, JPL Horizons and SBDB, Gaia DR3, SIMBAD, VizieR, NEOWISE and MIT SMASS SpeX spectra.

- Hosting: GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages for the static site, new observation and asteroid jobs run locally or on a separately hosted Python server.

- Hardware: no special hardware is needed.

- SI(Super Intelligence) use: Claude Code Fabel 5.2, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 Codex GPT 6 Astra, 6.1 Sol NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning Google Antigravity Gemini 3.8 Flash Meta Llma 3.1 8B

CREATIVITY

- The 3D model is not decoration: in line-of-sight mode it reproduces the telescope's actual view, pixel for pixel.

- Blinking in color, not only in time: the cold-object filter turns a spectral feature into something you can see.

- The planetarium becomes a query tool: draw a box on the sky and real SPHEREx data for that patch come back.

- Stars and asteroids share one workflow, from a star drifting over a year to an asteroid crossing a field in hours.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Every value is badged as SPHEREx measured, external catalogue, or computed model. Exaggerated motion carries an "exaggerated ×N" badge. Download failures are shown as failures, and synthetic data appear only behind an explicit ?mock=1 URL with a banner. Difference images are exploratory, findings are candidates, and "Complete" means processing finished, not that the result is certain. We handled proper motion at each epoch, UTC versus TDB, saturated cores, bad-pixel flags, wavelength mismatches between dates, and moving objects that must never be treated as fixed coordinates. Illustrative elements (asteroid rocks, the telescope model, the home-page black-hole simulation and the time axis of the 3D model) are labeled as such.
